content: In 2015, a series of group sessions lasting 60 to 90 minutes were conducted to promote the well-being of children and mothers. These sessions focused on key topics such as the use of play materials, gentle discipline, dietary diversity, hygiene, and sanitation. Demonstrations were provided to teach parents how to engage in play and communication with their children, as well as to illustrate appropriate food quantities. For maternal well-being, the sessions emphasized strengthening primary relationships and included separate and joint sessions for mothers and fathers. A control group on a waitlist received services from Plan Uganda, which included nutrition education on dietary diversity. In a 2013 study on iron deficiency anemia (IDA), a two-arm trial was conducted. One arm involved psychosocial stimulation through weekly home visits by play leaders, who demonstrated how to use toys and interact with children. Families were also provided with toys and books. The nutrition intervention included weekly provision of a 35 mL bottle of ferrous sulfate syrup to children with IDA for six months. Another 2013 trial had three arms, with one integrated arm combining responsive complementary feeding and play group programs. Mothers received 11 nutrition education messages, 8 messages on responsive feeding, and 8 on age-appropriate play-based stimulation, along with toys, delivered through 30 home visits. The nutrition-only arm provided 11 nutrition education messages through home visits. The control group received routine Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS), which included center-based nutritional supplementation, home counseling on breastfeeding and complementary feeding, monthly growth monitoring, and informal preschool education for children aged 3 to 5 years. In a 1981 six-arm trial, one integrated arm received both a maternal education program and weekly food supplements from the third trimester of pregnancy until the child reached three years of age. Another group participated in the maternal education program without supplementation, focusing on enhancing environmental stimulation for children. Three other arms received weekly food supplementation during different time periods, including bread, milk, protein, vitamins, and minerals. A 2015 four-arm trial used a 2x2 factorial design to evaluate responsive stimulation and enhanced nutrition interventions. The responsive stimulation intervention involved home visits and group sessions to improve caregiver sensitivity and responsiveness through developmentally appropriate play activities. The enhanced nutrition intervention included responsive feeding messages and the distribution of multiple micronutrient powders for children aged 6–24 months to address prevalent deficiencies. Standard care was provided through the Lady Health Worker Program. Meta-analyses of child outcomes compared combined nutrition and caregiving interventions against standard care, caregiving interventions alone, and nutrition interventions alone. Child outcomes assessed included cognitive, language, motor, and socioemotional development, as well as growth indicators like height-for-age (HAZ), weight-for-age (WAZ), and weight-for-height (WHZ). Most evaluations used the Bayley Scales of Infant Development (BSID). The overall quality of evidence was graded as low, with no significant benefits observed for child growth outcomes. However, combined interventions showed significant improvements in cognitive, language, and motor development compared to usual care or nutrition interventions alone. Subgroup analyses revealed that combined interventions were more effective in malnourished children than in universally implemented studies. While no consistent evidence of adverse effects was found, cost data for interventions were limited. Policymakers require more research on cost-effectiveness and implementation strategies. Research gaps identified include limited studies on responsive caregiving in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs), insufficient focus on overnutrition, and a lack of standardized tools for assessing child and caregiver outcomes. Additionally, there is a need for more data on caregivers other than mothers and large-scale studies to inform evidence-based planning for nurturing care programs.
